# The canonical register: Nt

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Nt, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Nt to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The attested form is **𓈖𓏏𓋌**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Nt**.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: “NAY-ith” The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *neith* is *not false — it is a fallback*, and the register is exact about what that means. In systems that cannot carry diacritics (legacy databases, older tooling, parts of the address-bar pipeline) the flattened form is the accepted vehicle, and the rulebook names it explicitly as the final rung of the fallback hierarchy: full restoration first, circumflex where attested, macron-only by the academic standard, an attested variant, and only then plain ASCII.

What the fallback status forbids is promotion: *neith* may carry the name where marks are impossible, but it may not *represent* the name where marks are possible.  A fallback is a vehicle, never the primary.

Now to the forms that provoked your letter. As for *neit*: it comes from the anglicized respelling — the name written the way English guesses it sounds, and it fails because rewrites attested consonant clusters to fit English spelling habits; every cluster simplified this way erases a letter the sources write

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. Neith merges with the great mother-goddesses — Mut, Hathor, Nut — and in the Roman period with Athena, whose war-and-craft profile fit her uncannily; the Greeks of Sais simply called her Athena.  The identification was so natural that Herodotus describes her Sais temple in Athenian terms.

And it never stopped working. Her Sais oracle became a proverb of ancient wisdom, quoted from Plutarch to the Renaissance Hermetica; ‘lifting the veil of Isis (Neith)’ passed into modern language as the image of unveiled nature.  In Egyptology she anchors the study of Predynastic religion — her crossed-arrows sign is among the earliest divine emblems known.

## The Convention's Own History

Egyptological transliteration exists because hieroglyphs write consonants, not vowels. The characters ꜣ (aleph) and ꜥ (ayin) are consonants — a glottal reed and a pharyngeal grip — and rendering them as vowels does not "simplify" the name, it deletes consonants from it. The conventions in use descend from nineteenth-century decipherment and the standardized Manuel de Codage: ḥ, ḫ, ḏ, ṯ each mark a distinct consonant the Egyptian wrote and a modern reader must not merge. When this register defends them, it defends the principle that a writing system older than the alphabet gets to keep its consonants.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Nt** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Nt** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *neith* is sanctioned as the fallback vehicle and nothing more. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Nt** stands at [/neith/](/neith/).

The docket for this ruling: 1 false form ruled against, *neit* first on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 5 cited sources — Esna temple hymns (the great Neith cosmogonies), Contendings of Horus and Seth (Neith’s oracle), Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (the veiled image of Sais).
